newsitem.title: USA: Nations slide toward water conflicts.
newsitem.headline: Nations slide toward water conflicts.

text.p: The world is sliding toward major environmental clashes because people have failed to use resources like water more wisely since the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, the leader of the summit said on Wednesday.
"Environment and resource-related issues are going to become tremendous sources of conflict," said Maurice Strong, who was secretary general of the landmark summit.
Strong said the struggle for resources in the future would turn on water rather than oil, and the strain on resources would trigger migrations into industrialised countries like never before.
"My view is water issues are going to actually overtake oil issues as primary sources of conflict in the Middle East. The same is true in Africa," he said.
"We will be experiencing what I have often called the deferred costs of apathy," he said at a news conference.
Strong chairs the Earth Council, an international group pressing for implementation of accords from the summit.

In a report released ahead of a conference of private organisations and governments in Rio March 13-19 to advance the 1992 agreement, the Earth Council said governments failed to live up to their pledges to protect the environment, and narrow the gap between rich and poor.
"The basic trends in our economic life which have caused the environmental problems have not fundamentally changed," Strong said. "Progress, yes. But overall we continue to slip back."
The groups meeting in Rio in March planned to press for more action by businesses, trade associations and other private groups, and more action by governments to reflect the true value of resources.
"We want to drive home to finance ministers that they need to reexamine their budget processes," Strong said.
Strong said the Earth should be run more like a business, "with its real assets -- its biological resources, its life-support systems" valued economically.
The Earth Council report listed a series of bad trends which it said should be reversed.
It said more than 100 nations were worse off now than 15 years ago, and about 1.3 billion people earned less than $1 a day.
"About 1.5 billion people live with dangerous air pollution, 1 billion live without clean water, and 2 billion without sanitation," the report said.
"Our environmental future is now basically hostage to what happens in the developing countries," Strong said.
